lit.\u0027\u003cdiv class=\"card-kicker\"\u0:
"
Qualitative score: 3 − 1.5·|Δhardness| + ionic (hard–hard) or covalent (soft–soft) terms
"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn una reacción de \u:
"

In an exchange reaction A₁B₁ + A₂B₂ ⇌ A₁B₂ + A₂B₁, the equilibrium shifts toward the side with the higher total score. Try Al³⁺/Hg²⁺ with O²⁻/S²⁻: aluminum ends up with oxygen and mercury with sulfur.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEntre ambos extremos:
"

Between the two extremes are borderline species (Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺; Cl⁻, Br⁻). Go through the table of cations and bases and see how radius and cloud change. The criterion is qualitative: hardness is not a directly measurable quantity but a guide based on trends.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa \u003cb\u003egeoqu:
"

Geochemistry follows HSAB: hard cations (Al³⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe³⁺) occur as oxides and silicates (bauxite, olivine); soft ones (Hg²⁺, Cu⁺, Ag⁺, Pt²⁺) as sulfides (cinnabar HgS, chalcocite Cu₂S). This guides extraction: sulfides are roasted; aluminum oxides are dissolved in base.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa regla de Pearson::
"

Pearson's rule: hard acids prefer hard bases and soft acids prefer soft bases. Hard–hard bonds are mainly ionic (charge/radius); soft–soft bonds are more covalent (polarizability). Choose an acid and a base: the qualitative score rises when both match and the sphere moves closer.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003ePearson clasificó áci:
"

Pearson classified acids (electron-pair acceptors) and bases (donors) as hard or soft. Hard species are small, highly charged and weakly polarizable (Al³⁺, F⁻, OH⁻); soft ones are large, low-charged and highly polarizable (Hg²⁺, Ag⁺, I⁻, S²⁻). The spheres show size and the translucent “cloud” shows polarizability.

"
